title: South Harbor
summary: South Harbor and Indian Neck are connected to Corchaug homelands and a contested record of Native land in Southold. Later sources describe Southold setting aside a 120- or 125-acre tract at South Harbor in 1685. Corchaug family tradition says families were pushed from that tract around 1690, while a 1763 petition stated that Corchaug descendants had lived at Indian Neck since 1691 and had never settled at South Harbor.
activity_update_summary: Added pre-1685 Corchaug land-pressure context, carefully attributed family tradition about South Harbor, the 1763 Indian Neck petition, and expanded source connections.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Corchaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: The 1763 petition preserves Corchaug descendants' own challenge to a land history written largely through Southold's records. Their statement of continued residence at Indian Neck rejects the idea that Native families simply disappeared or abandoned the North Fork. Read alongside the 1685 record and later family tradition, it makes this a history of continuing presence, memory, and legal resistance—not only a colonial allotment.
introduction_content: South Harbor and Indian Neck belong to Corchaug homelands on the North Fork. English settlement at Southold began in 1640, followed by land transactions, fencing, and livestock that narrowed Native access to planting grounds and other resources. In 1685, Southold recorded setting aside land at South Harbor for Native use; later sources describe the tract as either 120 or 125 acres. Corchaug family tradition says remaining families were pushed from that land around 1690 and that Yoopsag, a daughter of Momoweta, resisted moving. A September 1763 petition provides the clearest Native legal account: Corchaug descendants told Lieutenant Governor Cadwallader Colden that they had lived at Indian Neck since 1691 and had never settled at South Harbor. Reading the petition with the town record and family tradition shows why the history cannot be told from colonial documents alone.
